name: Kira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small firm out in the valley, six of us, run by a man called Arne Dahl. We put up timber-frame houses and do roofs, mostly for farmers and people building holiday cabins. My part is the framing and the roof timbers, cutting rafters and fitting them up on the walls. I like being up on the ridge on a clear morning with the whole valley below. The cold wears me out now, and the drive, it's fifty minutes each way on the gravel road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Fifty minutes each way. What does home look like at the end of that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tom, my husband, is home most of the day. He worked in the forest for years until his hip went, and now he's on disability money, so I'm the main wage. Our daughter Freya lives five hours away and our son Nils works at the fish plant on the coast. I've got a phone with buttons, I don't do apps or any of that AI business. We've maybe ten days of money in the bank, and Arne's is the only builder this side of the pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, nothing to it. Arne would say the same over coffee in the van. I don't go online, so that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That suits me fine. Nothing changes for us, Arne keeps getting his cabin jobs, I keep cutting rafters. The money's still thin, but it was thin before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. Same van, same road, same jobs. I'd try to get through another eight or nine winters and then see what we can manage on two small pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather forecast that says more of the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money was thin before. What makes it thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arne pays what he can, which isn't much, because the farmers bargain hard. Tom's money just about covers his share. The van eats a lot in diesel and tyres on that road. We don't go without food, but a broken boiler would be a real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about AI you'd notice even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Arne's daughter does his quotes on the computer with it, she mentioned that once. It doesn't touch me. A rafter doesn't care what the computer thinks, it's either cut right or it's firewood.

S0.say: There you go, nothing to it. I'd say it to Arne over coffee in the van, and I don't go online.
S0.think: That suits me fine, nothing changes and I keep cutting rafters. The money's still thin, but it was thin before.
S0.do: Keeps going exactly as she is, same van, same road and same jobs. Aims to get through another eight or nine winters and then manage on two small pensions.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast of more of the same.
S0.quote: A rafter doesn't care what the computer thinks, it's either cut right or it's firewood.
S0.fieldNote: Kira is short-spoken and practical and simply doesn't engage with AI at all. In this picture she's calm because nothing touches her daily work. Her money is very thin and she is the main earner, which will matter in the harder pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, there's always something new. I wouldn't make a fuss. If someone asked, I'd say I'll keep doing my work and let the young ones worry about the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But honestly, this one worries me. They already make whole wall panels in a factory in town and truck them out. If machines take more of that, Arne either buys panels or loses jobs to firms that do, and either way they need fewer people cutting timber on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't go learning computers, I'm not built for it. I'd cut back, no more takeaway pizza on Fridays, and keep the heating lower, and I'd wait and see what Arne decides. If he starts buying panels, I'd ask to be the one who fits them, because someone still has to lift them into place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a tight feeling. I'm the wage, so if I go, we all go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not built for computers. What's happened when you've tried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son set up a smartphone for me once, three years ago. I couldn't make it ring when I wanted and it rang when I didn't. After two weeks I gave it back and went back to buttons. I felt like a fool, and I don't like feeling like a fool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if I go, we all go'. What would that look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom can't work, so it'd be his little bit of money and nothing else. We'd have to ask Freya for help, and she's got her own kids. I'd rather not think about it, to be honest, so mostly I don't.

S1.say: It's how things go, there's always something new, and I wouldn't make a fuss. I'd keep doing my work and let the young ones worry about computers.
S1.think: Factory wall panels already come out from town, and more machines means fewer people cutting timber on site. Either Arne buys panels or he loses jobs to firms that do.
S1.do: Cuts Friday takeaways and keeps the heating lower, and refuses to learn computers. Waits to see what Arne decides and asks to be the one who fits factory panels if he switches.
S1.feel: Anxious and tight, because she's the main wage and if she goes, the household goes.
S1.quote: I'm the wage, so if I go, we all go.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is a shrug, but privately she has already worked out how factory panels squeeze her job. She avoids thinking about the worst case on purpose. Her refusal to learn new tech comes from one bad experience that made her feel foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say nothing much, honestly. Maybe that someone should have thought it through before letting it loose. I'm not one for shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be the end of us. I'd be 60, no savings, Tom on disability, and the only builder this side of the pass replacing people with machines. There's no other job in the valley for a woman of 60 who cuts rafters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd do, that's the truth. I'd apply for whatever money the government gives out, and I'd have to ask Freya if we could move nearer to her, maybe into a flat in her town. We'd sell the old trailer and Tom's chainsaws. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic. Like being on the roof when the ladder's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years before it arrives. Would you do anything in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every hour Arne gives me, I suppose, and hope he's slow to buy the machines. He's not one to rush, he still uses a pencil. But if the big firms in town undercut him, he won't have a choice. Two years isn't long enough to save anything when you're saving nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move near Freya. How would Tom feel about leaving the valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate it. He grew up there, his dad's buried there, he knows every tree. He'd come, because what else, but something would go out of him. That's the bit I can't stand to picture.

S2.say: Someone should have thought it through before letting it loose. I'm not one for shouting, so I'd mostly say nothing.
S2.think: It'd be the end of us, at 60 with no savings, Tom on disability and the only local builder bringing in machines. There's no other job in the valley for a woman of 60 who cuts rafters.
S2.do: Works every hour Arne offers in the two years before and applies for any government money. Plans to sell the trailer and Tom's chainsaws and ask her daughter if they can move to a flat in her town.
S2.feel: Panic, like being on the roof with the ladder gone.
S2.quote: He grew up there, his dad's buried there, he knows every tree.
S2.fieldNote: She has no plan and says so plainly, which is itself telling. She blames nobody in particular, just a vague 'someone' who should have thought it through. The idea of taking Tom away from the valley hurt her more than the loss of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd keep quiet. Maybe I'd say to Arne we should think about what we'll do. That's about as far as I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63. That's not pension, but it's closer. If Arne keeps going on the small jobs, the repairs and old barns that need a person, I might just hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Arne I'll take the repair jobs, the old barn roofs, the awkward stuff. I'd put the bit of money from selling the trailer in the bank and not touch it, and cut back on the Friday food and the heating like I said. Mostly I'd keep my head down and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but there's a bit of time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the old barns? What makes that work different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing's straight in an old barn. Every beam's a different size, half of them are rotten, and you only find out when you open it up. I'd like to see a machine work out where Mr Holm's grandfather put the nails. You need someone who's done it a hundred times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try learning anything new with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I know you're asking because it'd help. But I'd waste the five years trying to be something I'm not, and I'd be worse at my own work while I did it.

S3.say: I'd keep quiet, maybe just say to Arne that we should think about what we'll do. That's as far as I'd go.
S3.think: By 63 I'd be closer to a pension. If Arne keeps the small repair and old barn jobs that need a person, I might hang on.
S3.do: Asks Arne for the repair and old barn roof jobs and keeps working with her head down. Banks the money from selling the trailer, cuts back on food and heating, and declines to learn anything new.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, but with a little time to breathe.
S3.quote: I'd like to see a machine work out where Mr Holm's grandfather put the nails.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her a narrow path, the awkward repair work on old barns, and she clings to it. She turns down the idea of learning something new and explains why clearly, not just stubbornly. She still loses sleep because the plan depends entirely on Arne.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. I wouldn't say much else. People talk too much about things that haven't happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, and people think that means I'm safe. But we can't stop at 66, not with Tom's money as it is. I always planned to work till 70 if my body lets me, so this still lands on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and put a little aside when I can, even fifty a month. I'd wait and see how things go before changing anything. If Arne got machines in, I'd ask to stay on for the repair work for my last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. It's further off, but it's still coming for my last years of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you planned to work until 70. Why 70?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the pension alone won't cover us both with the van and the house. Every year I work past 66 is a year we're not eating into nothing. Arne's 64, I've already told him I'll outlast him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Nils and Freya to do with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nils should get out of the fish plant before the machines get in there, that's my view. Freya's a teacher, she'll be all right I think. I'd tell Nils, but he doesn't listen to me, he never has.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. People talk too much about things that haven't happened.
S4.think: At 68 people think I'm safe, but we can't stop at 66 on Tom's money. I always planned to work till 70, so this still lands on me.
S4.do: Keeps going as normal, puts aside even fifty a month when she can, and waits to see how things go before changing anything. Plans to ask Arne to keep her on for repair work if he brings in machines.
S4.feel: Quietly anxious, because it still reaches her last years of work.
S4.quote: Arne's 64, I've already told him I'll outlast him.
S4.fieldNote: Unlike most people her age, ten years doesn't make her safe, because she can't afford to retire at pension age. She defaults to waiting and seeing rather than acting early. Her advice to her son shows she sees the threat clearly even if she won't change herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. There's nothing I could do in two years. What would help is if the government made sure people over 60 in the trades could get the pension early if their work goes, and help for people like Tom who can't work. I don't need courses, I need the money to not stop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the country places. Everyone talks about cities. Out where we are, one firm closing is the whole valley's work gone, and nobody's going to build a robot factory in the valley.

headlineQuote: I don't need courses, I need the money to not stop.
portrait: Kira Larsen is a 58-year-old framing and roofing carpenter at a six-person firm in a rural valley, the main earner for a husband on disability money, with about ten days of savings and a phone with buttons. She is short-spoken, refuses to learn new technology after one embarrassing try, and rarely blames anyone. Plateau leaves her calm, Steady Disruption makes her anxious, and AGI by 2028 leaves her panicked, with no plan beyond moving near her daughter and taking Tom from the valley he loves. Even with ten years she stays anxious, because she always planned to work until 70.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's nothing she could do in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Early pension access for over-60s in the trades whose work disappears, and support for people like Tom who can't work.
